title: Choose life (Deuteronomy 30:15–20)
hook: life and death set before you: choose life
carry: the word is very near you

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shema: hear, O Israel, and love God with heart, soul and strength. Your line was with all thy heart. Did you say it, or name it, lying down? Day three hundred eighty-eight.

The day after Ash Wednesday, when Catholics have just had ashes on their foreheads and heard remember you are dust, the Church opens the Bible to this page. Moses is near the end of his last speech. He's said everything. All the laws, all the stories, all the warnings. And now he does what a good teacher does at the end of a long course. He takes it all and boils it down to one choice. Not a hundred rules. Two roads. And he tells them, in front of witnesses, which one to take.
screen: `THE DAY AFTER ASH WEDNESDAY.` → `THE END OF MOSES'S SPEECH.` → `TWO ROADS.`

segments.voice: First, the nearness. Just before this, Moses says that this commandment isn't too hard for you or far away. It isn't up in heaven, so that you'd need someone to go get it. It isn't across the sea. The word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it. Second, the choice. "I call heaven and earth to witness this day, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Choose therefore life, that both thou and thy seed may live." Notice what Moses doesn't do. He doesn't pretend there's no choice. He doesn't make it for them. He lays both roads out plainly and then, like a parent, can't help saying which one he hopes they'll take. Third, what life means. In Hebrew, the word for life, chayyim, is plural, as if life were never just one thing. The toast l'chaim, to life, comes from it. And Moses says what that life is: loving the Lord, listening to his voice, holding fast to him, for he is your life and the length of your days. Choosing life, in Moses's words, isn't only staying alive. It's holding fast to the God he calls your life. Fourth, how Catholics carry it. Pope John Paul the Second drew on passages like this in his letter on the Gospel of Life, teaching that every human life, from its beginning to its natural end, is a gift to protect. And the Church puts this reading at the start of Lent, a season of small choices, every one of them a road.
screen: `THE WORD IS VERY NEAR YOU.` · `LIFE AND DEATH, BLESSING AND CURSE.` · `CHAYYIM: LIFE, IN THE PLURAL.` · `HE IS THY LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make one choice for life. Settle, and breathe. Look at the day ahead and find a fork in it, a small one. Go to bed on time or scroll till two. Call your mother back or let it go another week. Eat something real, or skip it again. Say the kind thing, or the sharp one. Visit the sick neighbor, or don't. Pick one fork. See both roads clearly, the way Moses laid them out. Then choose the one that has more life in it, for you or someone else. If you pray, you can ask for help to keep that choice. If you don't, just commit to it quietly. The bell holds the time.
Choose life. Moses's final charge: life and death set before you, and a plea to choose life, and the God who is life. Today's word.
Your line: the word is very near you. Today, at one small fork, notice both roads, and take the one with more life in it. Day three hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: Deuteronomy 30:15–20 is read at Mass on the Thursday after Ash Wednesday, at the start of Lent, and Pope John Paul II's encyclical Evangelium Vitae (1995) draws on it in teaching the dignity of every human life.

fork.setup: you're Moses, at the end of your last speech. you've set life and death before the people. what's your final word?
options: choose life, that you and your children may live.
the choice is already made for you.
fork.reveal: he can't help himself: choose therefore life. and he names what life is: loving the Lord, for he is your life.

original.note: Hebrew: and you shall choose life. chayyim, life, is a plural word.

trapdoor: what you thought: a slogan on a bumper sticker.
what it means: Moses's last plea: two roads in plain view, and life means holding fast to the God who is your life.
what a scholar hears: Paul quotes the word is near you in Romans 10, and chayyim, life, is grammatically plural.
recall: walked in first, says Jewish tradition

sources.quoted: I call heaven and earth to witness this day, that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Choose therefore life, that both thou and thy seed may live.

sources.ref: Lectionary for Mass, Thursday after Ash Wednesday

notes: Thursday after Ash Wednesday: first reading Deuteronomy 30:15–20. Confirm.
Evangelium Vitae's use of Deuteronomy 30 (e.g., EV 28 and the encyclical's closing): stated generally as 'passages like this'. Confirm.
Chayyim as a plural form: standard grammar.
'Remember you are dust' at Ash Wednesday: one of the two formulas for the imposition of ashes.

Editor review (2026-10-01): cut the invented aside that Moses 'sounds almost like an apology for how long he's been talking'; 'choosing the God who is life' now attributed to Moses's words; Evangelium Vitae no longer said to be 'built around' this passage; 'forty days' count cut.
